content: When conducting searches for medical literature, it is possible to miss many relevant sources while being highly specific, as the search may only retrieve highly relevant sites. Some software tools allow the use of Boolean logic to link search terms, thereby increasing the specificity of the results. Boolean operators such as AND, OR, and NOT, named after the 19th-century British logician Charles Boole, instruct the computer on how to treat the relationship between search terms. For example, using AND requires both terms to appear in each reference, OR allows either term to be present, and NOT excludes references containing a specific term. Advanced search engines may also include tools like proximity operators (e.g., SAME or WITH) to specify how closely linked the terms must be within a reference. Additionally, wildcard symbols like the asterisk () can be used for truncation, allowing the search to retrieve all words beginning with a specific string of characters. For instance, entering arter will retrieve terms such as artery, arteries, and arterial. Most search systems ignore case sensitivity in keywords. Health information is one of the most frequently retrieved types of content on the internet. However, the quality of this information varies significantly due to the unregulated and constantly changing nature of the internet. Reliable sources include official websites from reputable organizations, peer-reviewed journals, government institutions, and educational institutions. These sites form the backbone of credible health information. Additionally, commercial medical information websites often compete by providing regularly updated content. Free access to medical journals is increasingly available through initiatives like Open Access Now, which advocates for unrestricted access to research information. Platforms such as PubMed Central, SciELO, and the Directory of Open Access Journals provide free, full-text, quality-controlled scientific and scholarly journals. The HINARI program, led by the World Health Organization, offers full-text journal access to registered users from eligible institutions in low-income countries. Users can search for journals alphabetically or by subject and access articles through PubMed or individual publisher websites. Various databases and resources, such as MEDLINE, EMBASE, and LILACS, provide comprehensive access to medical literature. These databases cover topics ranging from pharmacology and nutrition to regional health sciences. MEDLINE, for example, includes information from Index Medicus, Index to Dental Literature, and the International Nursing Index, among others. When writing references for scientific papers, it is essential to follow the guidelines of the journal to which the paper is being submitted. The Vancouver style, also known as the citation-by-reference-number system, is commonly used in medical journals. This system numbers references in the order they are cited in the text. Alternatively, the Harvard system (citation-by-author-and-date) identifies references by the author's name and publication year. The Bangkok Declaration on Health Research for Development emphasizes that health is a fundamental human right and that health research is critical for improving health, social, and economic development. The declaration highlights the importance of ethical research practices, gender equity, and the accessibility of publicly funded research. It calls for inclusive research systems that involve all stakeholders, including civil society, and stresses the need for coherent, coordinated strategies to address global health disparities.
